strengths: The behavioral benchmark is a meaningful contribution to evaluating human-like visual grouping. It extends a classical paradigm to 255 natural images and 1,020 image-condition combinations, with 72 participants, counterbalanced conditions, matched dot distances, and eye-tracking controls.

The experiments connect grouping accuracy, reaction-time prediction, and patch-level object structure across nine models. DINOv3 ViT-B achieves 91.9% grouping accuracy, and the strong performance of DINOv3 ConvNeXt provides useful evidence that object-centric representations are achievable beyond Transformer architectures.

Gram alignment provides a promising intervention beyond correlational model comparisons: all four supervised models improve in grouping accuracy and object-centricity, with behavioral-alignment improvements particularly evident for the Transformers.

The manuscript is clearly organized, illustrates the behavioral paradigm effectively, and appropriately connects its findings to perceptual-grouping research and prior self-supervised object-discovery methods. Its principal value is empirical understanding and behavioral evaluation rather than a new architecture.
weaknesses: The reaction-time evaluation does not establish generalization to unseen images. Section 4.1 describes cross-validation over trials, although each image contributes four conditions sharing the image and central-patch representation. Without grouping folds by image, training can expose the readout to other conditions from a test image. Image-disjoint evaluation is needed to distinguish transferable grouping representations from image-specific predictability.

The behavioral analysis lacks baselines that separate condition-level effects from image-specific grouping difficulty. Because the MLP is trained directly on reaction times, reproducing the same-object and distance effects is not independent evidence that these effects emerge in the representation. Condition-only and distance-based predictors, together with within-condition or residual reaction-time correlations, would establish what the models explain beyond the experimental design.

The noise-ceiling normalization in Section 4.1 is not justified. Correlation between two noisy subject-half averages is generally lower than the attainable correlation between a latent noise-free predictor and either half; simply dividing model-to-half correlation by half-to-half correlation therefore does not establish that 1.0 represents perfect noise-limited alignment. The paper should report raw correlations, the estimated reliability, a justified ceiling calculation, and uncertainty. Figures 4, 6, and 7 also lack uncertainty estimates for model comparisons; averaging seeds alone does not establish reliable differences.

The mechanistic interpretation of Gram alignment exceeds the controls in Section 4.3. Students receive additional ImageNet training and distillation from a substantially stronger teacher, but there is no matched classification-only fine-tuning control or alternative feature-distillation baseline. Consequently, the results do not isolate Gram structure as the specific cause of improvement. The claim that classification performance is maintained is also unsupported by reported classification results.

Claims that training objective matters more than architecture are confounded by differences in pretraining data, training recipes, and teacher supervision. Matching architecture does not control these factors, and Table 1's binary 'Large dataset' column is insufficient to characterize them. The results support an advantage for the evaluated DINO checkpoints, but not the stronger causal attribution to objective or the conclusion that scaling classification objectives is the wrong direction.

Important reproducibility information is missing: readout widths, optimization and regularization settings, reaction-time loss and preprocessing, model checkpoint identifiers and input resolutions, and the Gram loss, weighting, training schedule, and token correspondence procedure. No dataset/code release plan or benchmark access information is provided. These omissions materially limit both verification of the experiments and reuse of the behavioral benchmark.

The object-centric metric needs a precise definition and more restrained novelty claims. Section 4.2 describes TPR/FPR as proportions of active patches inside/outside the object, whereas conventional ROC rates divide by all positive/negative patches; Figure 5 appears consistent with the conventional definition. Equations should resolve this discrepancy and specify patch-boundary handling and curve aggregation. The claim that the metric requires no object-level supervision also needs qualification because evaluation uses COCO object masks. Applying ROC-AUC to established patch affinities is useful, but its methodological novelty is limited.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful question for computer vision: whether object-centric representations in foundation models predict human perceptual grouping difficulty. The behavioral benchmark and empirical analysis could be valuable independently of introducing a new algorithm.

The behavioral experiment is carefully designed in several respects: 72 participants, 255 experimental images with four conditions each, counterbalanced assignments, matched dot distances across same/different conditions, and eye-tracking-based fixation control. Extending the two-dot paradigm to natural scenes provides useful behavioral data.

The results provide converging descriptive evidence across grouping accuracy, reaction-time prediction, and patch-level object-centricity. DINOv3 ViT-B achieves 91.9% grouping accuracy, and the Gram-alignment experiment extends the analysis beyond comparisons of frozen pretrained models. The presentation and qualitative examples make the central hypothesis easy to understand.
weaknesses: The reaction-time evaluation does not establish generalization to unseen scenes. Section 4.1 describes cross-validation over 1,020 trials, although these comprise four conditions for each of only 255 images. Without grouping folds by image, training and test sets can contain the same scene and central patch representation, allowing the readout to exploit scene-specific difficulty. Image-disjoint evaluation is needed to support the principal behavioral-alignment result.

The paper does not isolate prediction of nuanced grouping difficulty from prediction of broad experimental conditions. Figure 4B reproduces condition means, but the readout is explicitly trained on human reaction times. Condition-only and distance-based baselines, within-condition correlations, and prediction of residual reaction times would establish whether representations explain the trial-level variation emphasized in Section 3.2 beyond the same-object advantage and distance effect.

The noise-ceiling normalization in Section 4.1 is insufficiently justified. Split-half human correlation measures reliability between two noisy estimates; it is not generally the maximum correlation between a model and either estimate. Dividing model-to-half correlations directly by this value does not establish that 1.0 represents perfect noise-limited alignment. Moreover, the human splits are not described as independent of the subjects contributing training targets. Raw correlations, the numerical reliability estimate, an appropriate ceiling calculation, and uncertainty intervals are needed. Figures 4A, 6, and 7 provide no uncertainty supporting model differences or intervention effects.

The conclusion that training objective matters more than architecture is stronger than the comparisons permit. The models differ in pretraining data, scale, training recipes, and distillation history, while Table 1 reduces dataset differences to a binary indicator. Matching architecture alone does not isolate objective. The results support an advantage for the evaluated DINO checkpoints, but attributing that advantage primarily to the objective requires controlled comparisons or narrower claims.

The Gram-alignment experiment lacks controls needed for its mechanistic interpretation. Additional ImageNet fine-tuning is combined with teacher distillation, without a fine-tuning-only baseline or alternative distillation control. Thus, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to Gram structure. Figure 7 also shows a large object-centric AUC increase for IN1K ConvNext with almost no behavioral-alignment improvement, qualifying the proposed relationship. The claim that classification performance is maintained is not accompanied by classification results.

The object-centricity metric needs clarification. Section 4.2 defines TPR and FPR as proportions of active patches inside and outside the object; literally, these are not standard ROC rates, whose denominators are all positive and all negative patches, respectively. Figure 5 suggests this may be a wording error, but the implementation must be specified. The claim that the metric requires no object-level supervision also needs qualification because evaluation explicitly uses ground-truth instance masks. Its methodological novelty is limited as an application of standard ROC analysis to feature affinities.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central modeling experiments. The manuscript omits readout widths, optimization and regularization settings, precise model checkpoints and preprocessing, and the Gram-distillation loss, weighting, and training schedule. It provides no code or behavioral-data availability statement. These omissions materially limit verification and reuse of the proposed benchmark. Overall, the promising dataset and descriptive trends do not yet outweigh the unresolved evaluation and causal-attribution concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision question: whether object-centric representations in foundation models predict human perceptual grouping. Connecting natural-scene psychophysics to dense feature structure is valuable independently of proposing a new architecture.

The behavioral experiment is thoughtfully controlled: 72 participants, fixation monitoring, counterbalanced conditions, matched dot distances across same/different judgments, and manual annotation checks. The 1,020 image-condition combinations across 255 experimental images substantially extend the cited small-scale paradigm.

The comparisons provide useful empirical evidence. DINOv3 ViT-B achieves 91.9% held-out grouping accuracy, compared with 70.6–72.2% for supervised ViTs, and DINOv3-distilled ConvNeXt substantially improves over its supervised counterparts. Training the grouping classifier on separate COCO training images is a strength.

The paper connects behavioral prediction, patch-affinity structure, and a representation intervention in a coherent narrative. Gram alignment improves object-centricity and grouping accuracy for all four tested supervised models, making the intervention a promising addition to the observational comparisons.
weaknesses: The reaction-time evaluation does not establish generalization to unseen images. Section 4.1 describes cross-validation over 1,020 trials, although each of the 255 images contributes four conditions. Unless folds are grouped by image, training and test sets can share image content and the identical central-patch representation. This permits learning image-specific difficulty and can inflate behavioral alignment. Image-disjoint cross-validation is necessary to substantiate the central prediction claim.

The behavioral analysis lacks controls that distinguish detailed perceptual alignment from learning broad task effects. The MLP is explicitly trained on human reaction times, so reproducing the same-object advantage and distance interaction is not strong independent evidence of emergent human-like behavior. Condition-only and spatial-distance baselines, together with within-condition or condition-residualized correlations, are needed to show prediction of the nuanced trial difficulty emphasized by the paper.

The noise-ceiling normalization is not justified. Section 4.1 divides model-to-half-sample correlations by the correlation between two participant halves. Under a standard independent-noise model, a perfect latent predictor correlates with a noisy half-sample approximately as the square root of split-half reliability, rather than reliability itself. Thus, the reported normalization does not generally make 1.0 a valid ceiling. Raw correlations, the measured reliability, an appropriately justified ceiling, and participant/image-level uncertainty should be reported; averaging seeds and subject splits does not replace confidence intervals.

The Gram-alignment intervention does not isolate the claimed mechanism. Models receive additional ImageNet classification training alongside distillation, but there is no matched classification-only fine-tuning control or alternative distillation control. Consequently, the experiment supports the usefulness of the combined intervention more clearly than the claim that Gram structure specifically drives behavioral alignment. The conclusion also asserts maintained ImageNet classification performance without reporting those results. Figure 7 shows that the largest grouping-accuracy gain occurs for IN1K ConvNeXt, contradicting the text's claim that Transformers improve more across all three metrics.

Claims about the training objective being more important than architecture exceed the controlled evidence. The checkpoints differ in pretraining data, scale, training recipes, and teacher access. Matching architecture alone does not isolate the objective, and DINOv3-distilled ConvNeXt inherits a transformer's supervision. The comparisons establish differences between model packages, but a causal ranking of objective versus architecture requires stronger controls or narrower wording.

The object-centric metric needs a precise definition. Section 4.2 describes TPR and FPR as proportions of active patches inside and outside the object, which would instead describe complementary fractions of predicted positives. The plotted curves suggest a conventional ROC calculation, so this may be a reporting error, but the implementation cannot be verified. The metric also requires ground-truth object masks, contrary to an unqualified claim of requiring no object-level supervision; that claim should distinguish representation training from evaluation.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the principal experiments and the proposed benchmark. The manuscript does not provide MLP widths, optimization and model-selection details, the Gram loss equation and weighting, fine-tuning schedules, or a data/code availability statement. These omissions, together with the unresolved evaluation and intervention controls, leave important concerns that outweigh the otherwise promising empirical contribution.

strengths: The main contribution is a useful empirical connection between dense visual representations and human grouping behavior. The natural-scene benchmark extends classical psychophysics to 255 images and 1,020 image-condition pairs from 72 participants.

The behavioral experiment includes strong controls: matched dot distances, counterbalanced conditions, eye-tracked fixation, randomized response mappings, and manual checks of object annotations. Supplementary accuracy and sensitivity analyses support task validity.

Several results converge: DINOv3 achieves 91.9% grouping accuracy, object-centric AUC correlates strongly with behavioral alignment across nine models (Spearman r=0.950), and Gram alignment improves supervised representations.

The supplementary linear-readout baseline, within-condition RT correlations, and CLS-distillation control address meaningful alternative explanations. The paper clearly explains the experimental progression and appropriately acknowledges related DINOv3 Gram-anchoring work.
weaknesses: The RT cross-validation splits trials rather than images (Section 4.1). Each image supplies four conditions with the same central feature, so training can contain other conditions from a test image. This permits exploitation of image-specific difficulty and does not establish generalization to unseen scenes. Both outer and inner splits should group all conditions of an image together; this could materially change the central results.

The noise-ceiling normalization is not justified. Correlation between two noisy subject-half means (0.42) is not the ceiling for a model predicting either half; a latent noise-free predictor can correlate more strongly. Under standard independent additive-noise assumptions, the corresponding Pearson ceiling involves the square root of reliability. Consequently, 0.348/0.42=0.83 should not be interpreted as proximity to the attainable human ceiling without an appropriate derivation or empirical estimator. Raw correlations preserve the ranking but support a more modest absolute-alignment claim.

Uncertainty in the principal model comparisons is largely unreported. Figures 4, 6, and 7 and Table 3 lack confidence intervals or paired tests for model differences and distillation gains. Averaging ten readout seeds does not quantify variability across images and participants. This matters for close comparisons such as DINOv2 versus DINOv3 ConvNext (raw r=0.324 versus 0.321) and the small behavioral gain for IN1K ConvNext after Gram alignment.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the controls. CLS distillation tests global-feature transfer, but does not distinguish Gram matching from other forms of dense teacher-feature transfer. Classification-only fine-tuning baselines are mentioned for ImageNet accuracy, without clearly reporting their grouping and RT outcomes. Furthermore, training data, recipes, and objectives vary across model families, limiting claims that the objective is the principal cause of alignment.

The object-centricity analysis does not establish that object organization specifically explains behavioral alignment beyond general dense-feature quality, spatial proximity, or semantic discrimination. Within-condition correlations are helpful, but simple spatial/appearance baselines and controls for grouping accuracy are missing. The cross-model association also rests on only nine related models. The claimed metric is a straightforward application of ROC analysis and requires ground-truth masks for evaluation, so the statement that it operates without object-level supervision needs qualification.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful supplementary details. Exact checkpoint identifiers, image preprocessing and patch-mask assignment, Gram-training duration, and the hyperparameter-selection search are not fully specified. The abstract states that code and data are available 'here', but the supplied PDF provides no usable link. This particularly limits the practical value of the proposed behavioral benchmark.

strengths: The behavioral benchmark is a meaningful contribution: 72 participants provide judgments on 255 natural images across four conditions, yielding 1,020 image-condition stimuli. Counterbalancing, distance matching, eye tracking, and manual stimulus screening provide useful experimental control. Its value does not depend on introducing a new architecture.

The paper connects dense visual representations to human reaction times rather than evaluating segmentation accuracy alone. The strong association between object-centricity and behavioral alignment across nine models (Spearman r=0.950) is an interesting empirical finding.

Several supplementary controls strengthen the evidence: linear readouts preserve the model ranking, within-condition correlations show that prediction extends beyond condition means, and raw correlations make the normalized results interpretable.

Gram distillation provides an intervention beyond observational model comparisons. Improvements in grouping and behavioral alignment, unchanged classification accuracy relative to matched fine-tuning baselines, and the unsuccessful CLS-distillation control support the relevance of spatial representation structure. The presentation is generally clear and appropriately connects this experiment to DINOv3.
weaknesses: The reaction-time evaluation does not establish generalization to unseen images. Section 4.1 describes splitting the 1,020 trials rather than grouping the four conditions of each image into the same fold. Consequently, training and test sets can share image content and the identical central feature vector, allowing the readout to exploit image-specific difficulty. Both outer and inner splits should hold out entire images. This is consequential because behavioral prediction is a central result, and the supplementary linear baseline uses the same splitting procedure.

The noise-ceiling normalization is not adequately justified. The correlation between two noisy participant-half averages (0.42) is a reliability estimate, whereas a noise-free predictor's attainable correlation with one half is generally related to the square root of that reliability under standard measurement assumptions. Dividing model-to-half correlations directly by 0.42 therefore does not establish a calibrated fraction of attainable human alignment. The raw correlations preserve the ranking, but the reported 0.83 and discussion of the remaining ceiling gap require a better-founded estimator and uncertainty analysis.

The model comparisons do not isolate training objective from data, training recipe, and teacher provenance. DINO generations differ substantially from the supervised baselines, and DINOv3 ConvNext is distilled. The introduction acknowledges incomplete separation, but later conclusions that the objective is the key factor, and that scaling classification objectives is not the path forward, exceed the controlled evidence.

Gram alignment supports transfer of useful dense structure, but does not uniquely identify object-centricity as the mechanism of behavioral improvement. CLS distillation is a global-representation control and does not distinguish Gram matching from other forms of dense feature distillation. Moreover, object-centric AUC improves substantially for IN1K ConvNext while behavioral alignment changes very little in Figure 7. Dense-distillation controls and analyses separating object structure from local appearance or spatial cues would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation.

Statistical and reproducibility reporting remains incomplete. The principal model rankings and Gram-alignment gains lack confidence intervals or paired significance assessments; averaging readout seeds does not establish uncertainty over images and participants. Exact checkpoint identifiers, several preprocessing choices, and Gram-training duration are also unspecified. The abstract promises code and data through 'here,' but the supplied PDF contains no usable link there. These omissions limit independent verification of the benchmark and results.

strengths: The paper makes a valuable empirical contribution connecting object-centric visual representations to human grouping behavior. Its significance lies in the behavioral benchmark and representational analysis, rather than a new segmentation algorithm.

The behavioral experiment is carefully designed: 72 participants, 255 experimental images with four conditions each, counterbalanced presentation, matched same/different dot distances, and eye-tracking enforcement of fixation. This substantially extends the classical paradigm to natural scenes.

Several findings converge: DINOv3 achieves 91.9% grouping accuracy, object-centric AUC correlates strongly with behavioral alignment across nine models (Spearman r=0.950), and Gram alignment improves supervised models. The convolutional DINOv3 comparison usefully demonstrates that these properties are not exclusive to Transformers.

The supplementary linear-readout baseline, within-condition correlations, CLS-distillation control, and classification-accuracy checks strengthen the evidence. In particular, within-condition RT correlations show that predictions capture more than differences between the four condition means.
weaknesses: The main RT evaluation does not establish generalization to unseen images. Section 4.1 describes splitting the 1,020 trials rather than grouping all four trials from each image into the same fold. Consequently, training can contain other conditions from a test image, including the identical central feature vector. This permits learning image-specific difficulty and may inflate behavioral alignment. Image-grouped outer and inner cross-validation is needed; this is the principal reason for my slight preference for rejection.

The noise-ceiling interpretation is problematic. Dividing model-to-half-sample correlation by the correlation between two noisy subject halves does not generally yield the fraction of an attainable ceiling: a predictor of latent mean RT can correlate more strongly with one half than the halves correlate with each other. Thus, the reported normalized score of 0.83 should not be interpreted as 83% of attainable alignment without further justification. Reporting raw correlations is helpful, and this issue does not change model rankings.

Uncertainty is insufficiently characterized for the central model comparisons and Gram-alignment gains. Figures 4A, 6, and 7 lack confidence intervals or paired tests; averaging readout seeds does not quantify uncertainty over images and participants. This matters especially for close model rankings and the small behavioral gain for IN1K ConvNext. The nine related checkpoints also provide limited independent evidence for a general relationship across architectures and objectives.

The mechanistic conclusions exceed the controls. CLS distillation tests transfer of global representations, but does not distinguish Gram matching from other forms of dense feature distillation. Likewise, unchanged ImageNet accuracy does not establish that classification-only fine-tuning leaves behavioral alignment unchanged. Training data and recipes remain confounded across model families, so claims that the objective is the key factor and that patch correlations are the specific active mechanism should be narrowed.

Some reproducibility and scope details need clarification. Gram-alignment training duration, exact checkpoint identifiers, image preprocessing, and patch-to-mask assignment are incompletely specified. The abstract's 'Code and data are available here' has no usable link in the supplied PDF. The metric explicitly requires ground-truth masks for evaluation, making the claim 'without requiring object-level supervision' ambiguous. Finally, the benchmark contains 255 selected scenes with overlapping central objects, which limits broader claims about natural-scene grouping.
